strengths: Complete 14-module architecture with clear responsibilities and interfaces
Async pub/sub communication pattern ensures loose coupling
All modules are marked as replaceable (except core: AgentRegistry, ModelRegistry, WorkflowEngine)
Well-structured with consistent tables for properties, responsibilities, interfaces
Covers modern AI orchestration patterns (vector memory, capability registry, fusion engine)
Extensibility paths defined for every module
weaknesses: No implementation code exists for any of the 14 modules — purely aspirational design
Several modules (Planner, Memory, Learning, Benchmark, Metrics) have no concrete implementation
No concrete API schemas or type definitions — only conceptual interfaces
No deployment topology, scaling strategy, or operational runbooks defined
Single WorkflowEngine orchestrator is a potential bottleneck and single point of failure
No authentication, authorization, or multi-tenant isolation model defined
No performance targets or SLOs specified for any module

strengths: Well-defined 3-stage pipeline (Classifier → Scorer → Selector) with clear separation of concerns
Scoring formula with explicit weights and well-reasoned factors (task_match, model_quality, availability, cost_efficiency)
Multiple routing strategies (default, cost_optimized, fastest, consensus, fallback) covering real use cases
Complete agent→model mapping matrix with fallback agents for every category
6 routing algorithms documented (RoundRobin, WeightedRandom, LeastLoaded, HistoryAware, CostAware, Consensus)
Well-defined input/output JSON schemas for the routing API
Plugin-based extensibility model for custom classifiers and strategies
weaknesses: Scorer formula weights (0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1) are arbitrary with no empirical justification
Classification relies solely on keyword matching — no ML or semantic classification
All primary agents default to Claude Sonnet 4-6 — zero model diversity at primary routing level
No caching layer for repeated mission classifications
No monitoring or alerting specifications for router degradation
No A/B testing framework for comparing routing strategy effectiveness

strengths: Complete 8-stage pipeline (Planner → Router → WorkflowEngine → Comparator → FusionEngine → Validator → Learning → Memory)
DAG-based execution model with topological sort and parallel execution
Clear error handling table with actions and fallbacks for 5 failure modes
5 execution modes (Sequential, Parallel, Consensus, Iterative, Fallback) covering diverse mission types
Well-structured JSON schemas for DAG nodes, assignments, comparison matrices, validation reports
Observability and logging requirements specified
Learning feedback loop closes the quality improvement cycle
weaknesses: Learning and Memory modules are aspirational — no concrete implementation exists
No retry logic or timeout values specified (only 'Retry 1x' without delay/backoff strategy)
No circuit breaker pattern for failing agents or models
Iterative mode could cause infinite loops without a max iteration guard
No priority inversion or deadlock prevention strategy for DAG execution
WorkflowEngine crash recovery relies on 'snapshots' but no snapshot frequency or storage mechanism is defined

strengths: Multi-provider support (Anthropic, Ollama, OpenAI, Google, Groq, Together, Mistral, DeepSeek) with 8 providers
Quality scores per task category for each model
Auto-detection for Ollama models via `ollama list`
4-tier fallback policy (immediate → secondary → degraded → queue)
Health check lifecycle with automatic deactivation after 3 consecutive failures
Well-defined model metadata schema with capabilities, latency, and cost
Clean public API surface (register, list, best_for, health, refresh, scores)
weaknesses: Claude Sonnet 4-6 is the top recommendation for all 5 task categories — critical single point of dependency
Cost data is vague ($, $$, $$$) with no actual token pricing
No model version pinning strategy — critical for reproducibility
No A/B testing or canary deployment framework for model updates
No rate limiting or token budget enforcement mechanism
Gemini 2.0 Flash with 1M context is mentioned but not integrated as a primary fallback anywhere

strengths: 9 well-defined agents with distinct roles, permissions, and recommended models
Temperature settings tailored to each agent's task (Architect 0.2, Builder 0.1, Research 0.4)
Permissions granularly assigned per agent
Lifecycle management (registration → discovery → assignment → execution → report → unregistration)
Free model alternatives provided for every agent
Consistent table format across all agent definitions
weaknesses: All 9 agents share the same primary recommended model (Claude Sonnet 4-6) — no model diversity
No agent priority or preemption model for handling concurrent missions
No agent output validation or quality gate before passing to next pipeline stage
No agent timeout or resource limit specifications
No description of agent-to-agent communication patterns

issues: opencode.json agents section descriptions differ from AGENTS.md descriptions (e.g., SUPRA-Architect: 'Concevoir l architecture...' vs 'Concevoir l architecture du système, produire des ADR...') — minor inconsistency in 2 agents
routing_rules.json uses the same model (claude-sonnet-4-6) for all 9 rules — no model diversity in routing

No schema validation or JSON assertion tests for any configuration file
AGENTS.md describes 9 agents but the workflow diagram at the bottom does not include SUPRA-Router explicitly in the pipeline flow — it shows 'Agents' as a collective step

swift_code_quality.review: ContentView.swift is a 3521-line monolithic struct violating the Single Responsibility Principle — it bundles state management, view logic, sidebar navigation, detail views, chat, and autopilot into one file. ControlCenterStore.swift (32 lines) is clean, well-structured with proper dependency injection (init with reader parameter), error handling, and @MainActor isolation. SupraControlCenterView.swift (314 lines) is well-composed with extracted subviews, reusable grid columns, and clean navigation patterns. The contrast is stark: the newer code follows modern SwiftUI patterns while ContentView.swift appears to be a legacy accumulation. The project has ~20 Swift files in SUPRA/ which suggests reasonable modularization overall, but ContentView.swift urgently needs decomposition. ControlCenterStore uses ArtifactReader but there is no protocol abstraction for the reader — testability is limited without a protocol.

critical: Decompose ContentView.swift (3521 lines) into smaller focused views — target <300 lines per file, extract SUPRASection views, chat views, sidebar, autopilot logic into separate files
Introduce model diversity in routing_rules.json — add free/open-source model alternatives as primary for non-critical tasks to reduce Claude API dependency and cost
high: Add protocol abstraction for ArtifactReader (e.g., `protocol ArtifactReading { func read() throws -> Snapshot }`) to enable testability of ControlCenterStore and SupraControlCenterView
Create unit tests for existing Swift code — no test files found in the SUPRA/ app directory
Implement at least the Router and Planner modules from the architecture spec as runnable code to validate the architectural design
Add a configuration JSON schema (JSON Schema) for opencode.json and validation CI to prevent configuration drift
medium: Standardize agent descriptions across opencode.json and AGENTS.md for consistency
Reduce SUPRA-Router permissions in opencode.json from full edit/bash to read-only with specific command allowlist
Add a max iterations guard to the review workflow's fix_loop to prevent infinite correction cycles
Document the circular dependency resolution strategy in the DAG executor before parallel execution is enabled
Pin model versions explicitly in model_registry.json to prevent silent model updates from breaking reproducibility
Populate .opencode/skills/ and .opencode/workflows/ with actual workflow definitions or remove the references

summary: SUPRA demonstrates a well-architected design with excellent documentation (avg 8.4/10 across 5 documents), a clean OpenCode integration, and successful end-to-end execution proof. The configuration layer is solid (8/10) with minor consistency issues. Swift code quality is mixed (7/10): newer components like ControlCenterStore and SupraControlCenterView are clean and idiomatic, but ContentView.swift is a 3521-line monolith requiring urgent decomposition. The architecture documents are detailed but remain entirely unimplemented as runnable code. The execution proof validates all previous repairs are verified. Critical recommendations focus on code decomposition, model diversity, and test coverage.
